questions.question: What are the most common Java threading interview questions and how do you answer them?
questions.title: Common Java Threading Interview Questions
questions.direct_answer: The most common Java threading interview questions are: (1) thread vs process (a process has its own memory; threads share a process's memory); (2) how to create a thread (extend Thread or implement Runnable; prefer Runnable); (3) synchronized vs Lock (synchronized is built-in and automatic; Lock is explicit, flexible, and supports tryLock/timeout); (4) wait/notify vs await/signal (wait/notify are on Object and need synchronized; await/signal are on Condition with a Lock); (5) what is a race condition (correctness depends on timing when threads share state without synchronization); (6) what is a deadlock (threads circularly waiting for each other's locks). A good answer names the trade-off and gives a concrete example.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can answer the canonical threading questions by naming the trade-off (e.g., synchronized vs Lock, race condition, deadlock) with a concrete example — not just definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining 'race condition' or 'deadlock' abstractly without a concrete scenario or the resolution (synchronization / lock ordering).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Know the canonical six: thread vs process, creating a thread, synchronized vs Lock, wait/notify vs await/signal, race condition, deadlock — name the trade-off and give an example.

sections.title: The Canonical Threading Questions
sections.content: Java threading interviews tend to ask the same core questions. (1) Thread vs process: a process has its own memory space; threads share a process's memory and are lighter. (2) How to create a thread: extend Thread or implement Runnable; prefer Runnable because it separates task from execution. (3) synchronized vs Lock: synchronized is built-in and automatic (lock released on exit/exception); Lock (ReentrantLock) is explicit, supports tryLock with a timeout and fairness, and needs manual unlock in a finally block. (4) wait/notify vs await/signal: wait/notify are methods on Object and require the caller to hold the object's monitor; await/signal are on a Condition tied to a Lock and offer multiple wait-sets. (5) Race condition: correctness depends on timing when threads share state without synchronization. (6) Deadlock: threads hold locks each other needs, circularly waiting. A strong answer names the trade-off and gives a concrete example.

sections.title: Threading Question Map
sections.content:
The canonical questions map to a few concepts: creation, mutual exclusion, coordination, and hazards.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q[Threading questions] --> C[Creation: Thread vs Runnable]
  Q --> M[Mutual exclusion: synchronized vs Lock]
  Q --> Co[Coordination: wait/notify vs await/signal]
  Q --> H[Hazards: race condition & deadlock]
```

sections.title: A race condition and a deadlock in code
Common Mistakes
items: Defining 'race condition' or 'deadlock' without a concrete example or the fix.
Not knowing that Lock.unlock() must be in a finally block (synchronized releases automatically).
Confusing wait/notify (Object + synchronized) with await/signal (Condition + Lock).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: The canonical six: thread vs process, creating a thread, synchronized vs Lock, wait/notify vs await/signal, race condition, deadlock.
Thread vs process: threads share a process's memory; processes have separate memory.
synchronized is automatic (released on exit); Lock (ReentrantLock) is explicit with tryLock/timeout and needs unlock in finally.
Race condition: timing-dependent correctness on shared state — fix with synchronization or atomics.
Deadlock: circular lock waiting — fix with consistent lock ordering.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Java threading interviews tend to ask the same core questions. Thread versus process: a process has its own memory space, while threads share a process's memory and are lighter. How to create a thread: extend Thread or implement Runnable, and prefer Runnable because it separates the task from execution. Synchronized versus Lock: synchronized is built-in and automatic, the lock is released on exit or exception, where Lock, ReentrantLock, is explicit, supports tryLock with a timeout and fairness, and needs manual unlock in a finally block. Wait-notify versus await-signal: wait and notify are on Object and require holding the object's monitor, while await and signal are on a Condition tied to a Lock and offer multiple wait-sets. Race condition: correctness depends on timing when threads share state without synchronization, fixed by synchronizing or using atomics like AtomicInteger. Deadlock: threads hold locks each other needs, circularly waiting, fixed by always locking in a consistent order. A strong answer names the trade-off and gives a concrete example, not just a definition.
